paras: The threatened lynching of John Coppedge took place in Nashville, Nash county, North Carolina, in July and September 1903, when local talk of lynching followed his arrest and later his sentencing for breaking into a widow's house. Officers moved him to the Wilson jail and, after his trial, guarded him overnight and took him to the state penitentiary, and no attack on him was reported. North Carolina papers covered the case chiefly as a story of the woman's courage, and the trial judge praised the county for letting the law take its course.

According to a Nashville correspondent of the Raleigh News and Observer, Coppedge, described as a Black man, entered the house of Mrs. Martha Hedgepeth, a widow living on Boddie street with her twelve-year-old daughter and invalid mother, through a window at daybreak on July 26, 1903. The account said Mrs. Hedgepeth woke, found him by her bed, and tried to shoot him with a pistol that misfired, then beat him on the head with it as he fled, and that he struck her in the face before breaking away.

Neighbors identified a coat left behind as Coppedge's, and Deputy Sheriff N. C. Warren and Chief of Police Collins arrested him at his home about a mile from town and brought him before Mrs. Hedgepeth, who identified him and begged the sheriff to let her kill him. He was jailed while "excitement was running high," and the correspondent reported "strong talk of lynching, as the people were deeply wrought up over the affair." Later that day the two officers took him to Wilson "for safe keeping," which the Gold Leaf said was done "fearing for the negro's safety." The paper added that he had confessed to entering the house "for meanness" and was a fugitive from Greene county.

Coppedge's case was one of three capital cases at the one-week Nash criminal term that opened on September 1 under Judge Ferguson. Through assigned counsel, the State accepted his submission to burglary in the second degree, and he was sentenced to life in the state prison at hard labor. As quoted from the Nashville Graphic, County Attorney B. H. Bunn then announced that the sheriff had reported "talk of lynching Coppedge last night," and Judge Ferguson cautioned the assemblage against any demonstration. Sheriff Warren posted about twenty-five guards at the jail overnight, and the next day Warren took Coppedge to the Raleigh penitentiary while a crowd gathered at the jail door to see him.

In passing sentence, Judge Ferguson commended the people of Nash for their "law-abiding spirit" and noted that "no unlawful violence had been done him." After sentencing, Coppedge told a Graphic reporter that he was grateful for the court's mercy but denied entering the residences of S. H. Griffin and others.

The coverage found is entirely from white papers, led by the Raleigh News and Observer, which headlined its first report "Lynching Was Feared" and its continuation "Let Me Kill Him Was Her Prayer." Its correspondent called Coppedge "the black devil," and an editorial the same day praised Mrs. Hedgepeth's pluck and advised that every woman "learn the use of a pistol." The story spread through a Raleigh wire to the Westminster, Maryland, Democratic Advocate as "Woman Whipped Negro" and through the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger, which credited the Wilson Times.

In September the News and Observer reprinted the Graphic's trial story under "Feared a Lynching" with the subhead "Would-be Rapist From Nash Brought to Raleigh," although the plea was to burglary. The Graphic itself doubted that the guards were needed, saying there was "little danger of harm coming to the prisoner." The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic reprinted the story, and a Norfolk digest in the Washington Evening Star reported that he was hurried to prison "there being strong threats of lynching," naming the woman as Hannah Hedgepeth. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

The News and Observer placed the entry at dawn on July 26, while the Gold Leaf said it occurred on "Saturday night," July 25. The local papers and court report name the woman Martha Hedgepeth, whereas the Evening Star digest calls her Hannah.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Coppedge
bases: Papers report 'strong talk of lynching' after his arrest in July and 'talk of lynching' on the night of his sentencing in September, each time met by moving or guarding the prisoner; no attack was made (A2, A4, A10, A11).

Coppedge was not killed or attacked; he was jailed, moved to Wilson, guarded, and delivered to the state penitentiary (A2, A10). The threat came from unnamed people angered by the accusation that he had entered a woman's house (A2, A4), but no group is described acting on it.

Two differently worded Nashville accounts agree on the entry, arrest and removal to Wilson for his safety (A1, A2, A4), and the September talk of lynching and transfer to prison appear in the Graphic account and in a separate Norfolk digest (A10, A11).

accounts.label: Nashville correspondent of the News and Observer
accounts.gist: Coppedge crept into the widow's room, fought her, struck her and fled; he was arrested, identified by his coat and wounds, jailed amid 'strong talk of lynching', and taken to Wilson; he is said to have confessed.

accounts.label: Gold Leaf's Nashville account
accounts.gist: The same incident placed on 'Saturday night'; Sheriff Warren took him to Wilson 'fearing for the negro's safety'.

accounts.label: Nashville Graphic, quoted by the News and Observer
accounts.gist: After the plea and life sentence, the sheriff reported talk of lynching, posted about twenty-five guards, and took Coppedge to Raleigh the next day; the paper doubted any real danger.

accounts.label: Norfolk digest in the Evening Star
accounts.gist: Coppedge was 'hurried to prison from Nash county, there being strong threats of lynching'.

accounts.label: Coppedge
accounts.gist: He protested his innocence at the woman's house, is said to have confessed later that day, and after sentencing denied entering other residences.

framing.detail: The News and Observer headlined 'Lynching Was Feared' and 'Let Me Kill Him Was Her Prayer', called him 'the black devil', and editorially urged every woman to keep a pistol, while reporting that the law would take its course.

The Graphic, via the News and Observer's 'Feared a Lynching', quoted the judge praising Nash for letting 'the law take its course' and doubted that guards were needed, though the headline called Coppedge a 'Would-be Rapist'.
Out-of-town papers carried condensed or reprinted versions under headlines such as 'Woman Whipped Negro'.
